name: Scarsdale diet

lead: The Scarsdale diet is a fixed 14-day meal plan of about 1,000 calories a day, built around lean protein, non-starchy vegetables and a little fruit, with sugar, alcohol and most fats excluded. It was devised by cardiologist Herman Tarnower of Scarsdale, New York and published in 1978.

Its appearance payoff is fast scale-weight loss and a leaner look, which is why people have used it ahead of weddings, photos or events. Proponents say the simple menu removes calorie counting; clinicians and nutrition writers note that early loss includes water and that regain is common.

paras: Followers eat the prescribed breakfast, lunch and dinner for two weeks with no substitutions, then move to a more flexible 'keep-slim' phase. Some versions of the programme alternate the strict plan with looser weeks. Protein is eaten without weighing, and only raw carrot or celery is allowed between meals.

Reported side effects include constipation, nausea, weakness and ketosis-related bad breath. Nutrition authors have described deficiencies including vitamin A and riboflavin, and note that very-low-calorie, high-protein plans suit people with certain kidney, heart or metabolic conditions poorly.

lead: The Scarsdale diet is a very-low-calorie, high-protein, low-carbohydrate weight-loss plan created in the 1970s by cardiologist Herman Tarnower and named for Scarsdale, New York, where he practised. It was set out in The Complete Scarsdale Medical Diet, co-written with Samm Sinclair Baker and published in 1978 [1][2].

People use it for rapid fat and scale-weight loss, usually to look leaner within about two weeks. The plan supplies about 1,000 calories a day over a fixed 14-day menu and is followed by a maintenance phase [1][2]. Medical writers classify it as a fad diet and describe both short-term loss and risks of deficiency, while one behavioural-treatment study in 1982 examined how a Scarsdale-style start affected later weight loss [2][3].

paras: The diet's strict phase lasts 14 days with a set menu: three meals a day, fruit such as grapefruit at breakfast, lean animal protein such as fish, poultry and eggs, and salads or non-starchy vegetables. Raw carrot or celery are the only permitted snacks, and one slice of protein bread is allowed daily, according to Grokipedia's description of the book [1]. Wikipedia characterises it as similar to the Atkins and Stillman diets but with more emphasis on fruit and vegetables, and meant to be followed for one to two weeks [2].
After the reduction phase a 'keep-slim' phase reintroduces a wider range of foods. The 1978 book also described alternating stricter and looser periods to maintain results [1].

Tarnower reportedly first gave the plan to cardiac patients as a short handout, on the view that weight loss would help their hearts, and it spread by word of mouth before the book appeared in 1978 [1]. The book became a bestseller. Wikipedia notes that sales rose further after Tarnower was murdered in 1980 by his former partner Jean Harris [2].

Wikipedia summarises several published critiques: weight lost on the plan is generally no more sustained than with ordinary calorie restriction; a 1988 review by nutritionist Elaine Feldman called high-protein, low-carbohydrate diets nutritionally deficient; and a 1986 paper by Howard and Roth noted shortfalls in vitamin A and riboflavin [2]. Reported side effects include constipation, nausea, weakness and ketosis-related bad breath [2].

Proponents emphasise the plan's simplicity and short duration, and Grokipedia describes the claim that the high protein content helps fullness and muscle retention during restriction, alongside the note that much of the early loss is water [1].

A 1982 paper in the Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology examined whether a greater initial weight loss on the Scarsdale diet affected subsequent weight loss in a behavioural treatment programme [3]. Beyond this, few trials of the plan itself are indexed.
